nodes.statement: Motivation Many numerical schemes have been proposed to approximate the solutions of nonlinear con\-vection-diffusion equations. In particular, finite volume methods have been proved to be efficient in the case of degenerate parabolic equations (see ). We also mention the combined finite volume-finite element approach for nonlinear degenerate parabolic convection-diffusion-reaction equations analysed in . The definition of the so-called local Péclet upstream weighting numerical flux guarantees the stability of the scheme while reducing the excessive numerical diffusion added by the classical upwinding.\\ On the other hand, there exists a wide literature on numerical schemes for the drift-diffusion equations. It started with 1-D finite difference methods and the Scharfetter-Gummel scheme (). In the linear pressure case (r(s)=s), a mixed exponential fitting finite element scheme has been successfully developed by F. Brezzi, L. Marini and P. Pietra in . The adaptation of the mixed exponential fitting method to the nonlinear case has been developed by F. Arimburgo, C. Baiocchi, L. Marini in and by A. Jüngel in for the one-dimensional problem, and by A. Jüngel and P. Pietra in for the two-dimensional problem. Moreover, C. Chainais-Hillairet and Y.J. Peng proposed a finite volume scheme for the drift-diffusion equations in 1-D in , which was extended in in the multidimensional case. C. Chainais-Hillairet and F. Filbet also introduced in a finite-volume scheme preserving the large time behavior of the solutions of the nonlinear drift-diffusion model.\\ Now to explain our approach, let us first recall some previous numerical results concerning the drift-diffusion system for semiconductors. The precise definitions of schemes considered will be presented in Section 2. We compare results obtained with three existing finite volume schemes: the classical upwind scheme proposed by C. Chainais-Hillairet and Y. J. Peng in , the Scharfetter-Gummel scheme introduced in and the nonlinear upwind scheme studied in .\\ In Figure , we present some results obtained in the case of a linear diffusion (r(s)=s). We represent the relative energy E and the dissipation of energy I obtained with the upwind flux and the Scharfetter-Gummel flux for a test case in one space dimension. We can observe a phenomenon of saturation of E and I for the upwind flux. In addition, we clearly observe that the energy and its dissipation obtained with the Scharfetter-Gummel flux converge to zero when time goes to infinity, which means that densities N(t) and P(t) converge to the thermal equilibrium. It appears that the Scharfetter-Gummel flux is very efficient, but is only valid for linear diffusion. Moreover, we can emphasize that contrary to the upwind flux, the Scharfetter-Gummel flux preserves the thermal equilibrium.\\ In Figure , we present numerical results obtained in the case of a nonlinear diffusion r(s)=s^2. We represent the relative energy E and the dissipation I obtained with the classical upwind flux and with the nonlinear upwind flux for a test case in one dimension of space. We still observe a phenomenon of saturation of E and I for the classical upwind flux. For the nonlinear flux, we clearly notice that the energy and its dissipation converge to zero when time goes to infinity.\\ Looking at these results, it seems crucial that the numerical flux preserves the thermal equilibrium to obtain the consistency of the approximate solution in the long time asymptotic limit. subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig1_1.eps subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig1_2.eps captionLinear case: relative energy E^n and dissipation I^n for different schemes in log scale, with time step Delta t=10^-2 and space step Delta x=10^-2. subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig2_1.eps subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig2_2.eps captionNonlinear case: relative energy E^n and dissipation I^n for different schemes in log scale, with time step Delta t=5.10^-4 and space step Delta x=10^-2. paragraph*Our aim is to propose a finite volume scheme for convection-diffusion equations with nonlinear diffusion. We will focus on preserving steady-states in order to obtain a satisfying long-time behavior of the approximate solution. The scheme proposed in satisfies this property but because of the nonlinear discretization of the diffusive terms, it leads to solve a nonlinear system at each time step, even in the case of a linear diffusion. The idea is to extend the Scharfetter-Gummel scheme, which is only valid in the case of a linear diffusion, for convection-diffusion equations with nonlinear diffusion, even in the degenerate case. Some extensions of this scheme have already been proposed. Indeed, R. Eymard, J. Fuhrmann and K. Gärtner studied a scheme valid in the case where the convection and diffusion terms are nonlinear (see ), but their method leads to solve a nonlinear elliptic problem at each interface. A. Jüngel and P. Pietra proposed a scheme for the drift-diffusion model (see ), but it is not very satisfying to reflect the large-time behavior of the solutions.

nodes.clean_text: Motivation Many numerical schemes have been proposed to approximate the solutions of nonlinear con\-vection-diffusion equations. In particular, finite volume methods have been proved to be efficient in the case of degenerate parabolic equations (see ). We also mention the combined finite volume-finite element approach for nonlinear degenerate parabolic convection-diffusion-reaction equations analysed in . The definition of the so-called local Péclet upstream weighting numerical flux guarantees the stability of the scheme while reducing the excessive numerical diffusion added by the classical upwinding.\\ On the other hand, there exists a wide literature on numerical schemes for the drift-diffusion equations. It started with 1-D finite difference methods and the Scharfetter-Gummel scheme (). In the linear pressure case (r(s)=s), a mixed exponential fitting finite element scheme has been successfully developed by F. Brezzi, L. Marini and P. Pietra in . The adaptation of the mixed exponential fitting method to the nonlinear case has been developed by F. Arimburgo, C. Baiocchi, L. Marini in and by A. Jüngel in for the one-dimensional problem, and by A. Jüngel and P. Pietra in for the two-dimensional problem. Moreover, C. Chainais-Hillairet and Y.J. Peng proposed a finite volume scheme for the drift-diffusion equations in 1-D in , which was extended in in the multidimensional case. C. Chainais-Hillairet and F. Filbet also introduced in a finite-volume scheme preserving the large time behavior of the solutions of the nonlinear drift-diffusion model.\\ Now to explain our approach, let us first recall some previous numerical results concerning the drift-diffusion system for semiconductors. The precise definitions of schemes considered will be presented in Section 2. We compare results obtained with three existing finite volume schemes: the classical upwind scheme proposed by C. Chainais-Hillairet and Y. J. Peng in , the Scharfetter-Gummel scheme introduced in and the nonlinear upwind scheme studied in .\\ In Figure , we present some results obtained in the case of a linear diffusion (r(s)=s). We represent the relative energy E and the dissipation of energy I obtained with the upwind flux and the Scharfetter-Gummel flux for a test case in one space dimension. We can observe a phenomenon of saturation of E and I for the upwind flux. In addition, we clearly observe that the energy and its dissipation obtained with the Scharfetter-Gummel flux converge to zero when time goes to infinity, which means that densities N(t) and P(t) converge to the thermal equilibrium. It appears that the Scharfetter-Gummel flux is very efficient, but is only valid for linear diffusion. Moreover, we can emphasize that contrary to the upwind flux, the Scharfetter-Gummel flux preserves the thermal equilibrium.\\ In Figure , we present numerical results obtained in the case of a nonlinear diffusion r(s)=s^2. We represent the relative energy E and the dissipation I obtained with the classical upwind flux and with the nonlinear upwind flux for a test case in one dimension of space. We still observe a phenomenon of saturation of E and I for the classical upwind flux. For the nonlinear flux, we clearly notice that the energy and its dissipation converge to zero when time goes to infinity.\\ Looking at these results, it seems crucial that the numerical flux preserves the thermal equilibrium to obtain the consistency of the approximate solution in the long time asymptotic limit. subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig1_1.eps subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig1_2.eps captionLinear case: relative energy E^n and dissipation I^n for different schemes in log scale, with time step Delta t=10^-2 and space step Delta x=10^-2. subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig2_1.eps subfigureincludegraphics[scale=0.45]fig2_2.eps captionNonlinear case: relative energy E^n and dissipation I^n for different schemes in log scale, with time step Delta t=5.10^-4 and space step Delta x=10^-2. paragraph*Our aim is to propose a finite volume scheme for convection-diffusion equations with nonlinear diffusion. The term overlineB_1 is treated like in , which leads to vert overlineB_1 vert leq M Vert q Vert_inftyVert overlineu_delta Vert_1,Ddm(Omega)=D_3. We apply Young's inequality for overlineB_2: for any alpha>0, we have leftvert overlineB_2 rightvert &leq &fracalpha2 sum_n=0^N_T Delta t sum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|L tau_sigmaleft(dr_K,sigma^nright)^2left(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr_K,sigma^ncothleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmaright)right)^2left(U_K^n+1-U_L^n+1right)^2\\ & & + fracalpha2 sum_n=0^N_T Delta t sum_K in T sum_sigma in E_ext,K^D tau_sigmaleft(dr_K,sigma^nright)^2 left(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmacothleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmaright)right)^2left(U_K^n+1-U_sigma^n+1right)^2\\ & &+ frac12alphaVert overlineu_deltaVert_1,D^2. By the hypothesis (H4), we have inf_s in [m,M]r'(s)>0. Then, using Lemma , the L^infty estimate on u_delta () and the hypothesis (H5), we have fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigma leq fracVert q Vert_inftydiam(Omega) inf_sin [m,M]r'(s), \, forall n in N,\, forall K in T, \, forall sigma in E_K. Moreover, since x mapsto x coth(x) is continuous on R, we obtain left(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmacothleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmaright)right)^2 leq D_4, \, forall n in N,\, forall K in T, \, forall sigma in E_K. First, using the expression () of the flux and Lemma , we have for all n geq 0, for all K in T and for all sigma=K|L in E_int,K F^n+1_K,sigmaleft(U^n+1_K-U^n+1_Lright) &=& fracm(sigma)q_K,sigma2left(left(U_K^n+1right)^2-left(U^n+1_Lright)^2right)\\ & & + tau_sigma r'(eta_K,sigma^n)fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2r'(eta_K,sigma^n) cothleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2r'(eta_K,sigma^n)right)left(U^n+1_K-U^n+1_Lright)^2. Through integrating by parts and using the hypothesis (H6), we get & &sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|L fracm(sigma)q_K,sigma2left(left(U_K^n+1right)^2-left(U^n+1_Lright)^2right)\\ &+&sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_Kin Tsum_sigma in E_ext,K^Dfracm(sigma)q_K,sigma2left(left(U_K^n+1right)^2-left(U^n+1_sigmaright)^2right) \\ & = & -sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_Kin Tsum_sigma in E_ext,K^D frac12int_sigmaq(x)cdot n_K,sigma\, ds(x) left(U_sigma^n+1right)^2=-D_5, and then B' geq inf_s in [m,M]r'(s)Vert u_deltaVert_1,D^2-D_5. Conclusion. Using A+B=0 and estimates (), () and (), we finally get for any alpha>0: left(inf_sin [m,M]r'(s)-fracalpha2D_4left(sup_sin [m,M]r'(s)right)^2right)Vert u_deltaVert_1,D^2 leq D_2+D_3+D_5+frac12alphaVert overlineu_deltaVert_1,D^2, thus for alpha < frac2 inf_sin [m,M]r'(s)D_4left( sup_sin [m,M]r'(s)right)^2, we obtain Vert u_delta Vert_1,D^2 leq D_1.

nodes.statement: Convergence of the scheme Now it remains to prove that the function u defined in Proposition satisfies Definition of a weak solution. The main difficulty in proving this comes from the fact that the diffusive and convective terms are put together in the Scharfetter-Gummel flux. Assume (H1)-(H7) hold. Then the function u defined in Proposition satisfies the equation ()-()-()-() in the sense of () and the boundary condition u-overlineu in L^infty(0,T;H^1_0(Omega)). Let psi in D(Omega times [0,T[) be a test function and psi^n_K=psi(x_K,t^n) for all K in T and n geq 0. We suppose that delta >0 is small enough such that Supp(psi) subset lbrace x in Omega; d(x,Gamma)>delta rbrace times [0,(N_T-1)Delta t[. Let us define an approximate gradient of psi by nabla^deltapsi(x,t)=left\lcl fracm(sigma)m(T_K,sigma)left(psi^n_L-psi^n_Kright) n_K,sigma & & if (x,t) in T_K,sigmatimes [t^n,t^n+1[,\,\ sigma=K|L, \\ fracm(sigma)m(T_K,sigma)left(psi_sigma^n-psi^n_Kright) n_K,sigma & & if (x,t) in T_K,sigmatimes [t^n,t^n+1[, \,\ sigma in E_ext,K. right. We get from that (nabla^deltapsi)_delta>0 weakly converges to nabla psi in (L^2(Omega times (0,T)))^d as delta goes to zero.\\ Let us introduce the following notations: B_10(delta) &=& -left(int_0^Tint_Omegaud(x,t)\,pa_tpsi(x,t)\, dx \, dt+int_Omegaud(x,0)\, psi(x,0) \, dxright),\\ B_20(delta) &=& int_0^Tint_Omegar'(u_delta(x,t-Delta t))\, nabla^deltau_delta(x,t)cdot nablapsi(x,t)\, dx \, dt,\\ B_30(delta) &=& -int_0^Tint_Omega ud(x,t)\, q(x) cdot nabla^deltapsi(x,t)\, dx \, dt, and varepsilon(delta)=-B_10(delta)-B_20(delta)-B_30(delta). Multiplying the scheme () by Delta t psi^n_K and summing through K and n, we obtain B_1(delta)+B_2(delta)+B_3(delta)=0, where B_1(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_Tsum_K in Tm(K)left(U_K^n+1-U_K^nright)psi^n_K,\\ B_2(delta) &=& -sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_K in T sum_sigma in E_Kfracm(sigma)q_K,sigma2cothleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr_K,sigma^nright)left(U^n+1_sigma-U^n+1_Kright)psi^n_K,\\ B_3(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_K in T sum_sigma in E_K m(sigma)q_K,sigmafracU_K^n+1+U_sigma^n+12psi^n_K. From the strong convergence of the sequence (ud)_delta>0 to u in L^2(Omega times ]0,T[), it is clear using the time translate estimate () that there exists a subsequence of (ud)_delta>0, still denoted by (ud)_delta>0, such that ud( \,cdot \, ,\, cdot \,-Delta t) longrightarrow u in L^2(Omega times ]0,T[) strongly as delta rightarrow 0, where u in L^infty(0,T;H^1(Omega)) is defined in Proposition . Moreover, thanks to hypothesis (H4), we have r' in C^1(R), and using the L^infty-estimate () we obtain that r'(ud(\,cdot \, ,\, cdot \,-Delta t))longrightarrow r'(u) in L^2(Omega times ]0,T[) strongly as delta rightarrow 0. Finally using this strong convergence and the weak convergence of the sequences (nabla^deltau_delta)_delta>0 to nabla u and (nabla^deltapsi)_delta>0 to nabla psi in (L^2(Omega times ]0,T[))^d, it is easy to see that varepsilon(delta)& longrightarrow & int_0^Tint_Omegaleft(u(x,t)\, pa_tpsi-r'(u(x,t))\, nabla u(x,t) cdot nabla psi+u(x,t) \, q(x) cdot nablapsiright) \, dx \, dt\\ & & +int_Omegau(x,0) \, psi(x,0)\, dx, as delta rightarrow 0. Therefore, it suffices to prove that varepsilon(delta) longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0 and to this end we are going to prove that varepsilon(delta)+B_1(delta)+B_2(delta)+B_3(delta) longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0.\\ Estimate of B_1(delta)-B_10(delta). This term is discussed for example in (Theorem 5.2) and it is proved that: |B_1(delta)-B_10(delta)| leq left[(T+1)m(Omega)MVert psi Vert_C^2(Omega times (0,T))right]delta longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. Estimate of B_2(delta)-B_20(delta). Using a discrete integration by parts, we write B_2(delta) = sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|Lfracm(sigma)q_K,sigma2cothleft(fracd_sigma q_K,sigma2 dr^n_K,sigmaright)left(U^n+1_L-U^n+1_Kright)(psi_L^n-psi_K^n). Then we rewrite B_2(delta)=B_21(delta)+B_22(delta)+B_23(delta), with B_21(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|L tau_sigmar'(U^n_K)left(U^n+1_L-U^n+1_Kright)(psi_L^n-psi_K^n),\\ B_22(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|Ltau_sigmaleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmacothleft(fracd_sigmaq_K,sigma2dr^n_K,sigmaright)-1right)dr^n_K,sigmaleft(U^n+1_L-U^n+1_Kright)(psi_L^n-psi_K^n),\\ B_23(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_TDelta t sum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|Ltau_sigmaleft(dr^n_K,sigma-r'(U^n_K)right)left(U^n+1_L-U^n+1_Kright)left(psi_L^n-psi_K^nright). Using the definition of tildeu_delta and nabla^deltau_delta, we rewrite B_20(delta) as B_210(delta)+B_220(delta) with: B_210(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_Tsum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|Lr'(U_K^n)fracm(sigma)m(T_K,sigma)left(U_L^n+1-U_K^n+1right)int_t^n^t^n+1int_T_K,sigmanabla psi(x,t) cdot n_K,sigma\, dx \, dt,\\ B_220(delta) &=& sum_n=0^N_Tsum_substacksigma in E_int \\ sigma=K|L\!\!\!\! left(r'(U^n_L)-r'(U^n_K)right)fracm(sigma)m(T_K,sigma)left(U_L^n+1-U_K^n+1right) int_t^n^t^n+1\!\!\!\!\! int_T_K,sigmacap L\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! nabla psi(x,t) cdot n_K,sigma\, dx \, dt. Now we prove that B_21(delta)-B_210(delta) rightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0 and B_22(delta), \, B_23(delta), \, B_220(delta)rightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0.\\ Estimate of B_21(delta)-B_210(delta). We have B_21(delta)-B_210(delta)=sum_n=0^N_Tsum_substacksigma in E_int \!\!\!\! m(sigma)r'(U^n_K)left[int_t^n^t^n+1\!\!\!\! left(fracpsi_L^n-psi_K^nd_sigma-frac1m(T_K,sigma)int_T_K,sigma\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! nablapsi(x,t)cdot n_K,sigma\, dxright)dtright]\!\!. Since the straight line overlinex_Kx_L is orthogonal to the edge K|L, we have x_L-x_K=d_sigman_K,sigma and then from the regularity of psi, fracpsi_L^n-psi_K^nd_sigma&=&nabla psi(x_K,t^n) cdot n_K,sigma+O(Delta x)\\ &=& nabla psi(x,t) cdot n_K,sigma+O(delta), \,\ forall (x,t) in T_K,sigma times left(t^n,t^n+1right). Then by taking the mean value over T_K,sigma, there exists D_6>0 depending only on psi such that leftvert int_t^n^t^n+1left(fracpsi_L^n-psi_K^nd_sigma-frac1m(T_K,sigma)int_T_K,sigmanabla psi cdot n_K,sigma \, dx right)dt rightvert leq D_6 delta Delta t, and then left|B_21(delta)-B_210(delta)right| leq delta D_6 sup_s in [m,M]r'(s)sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_intm(sigma)left|U_L^n+1-U_K^n+1right|. Since the straight line overlinex_Kx_L is orthogonal to the edge sigma=K|L for all sigma in E_int,K and the mesh is regular, there is a constant D_7>0 depending only on the dimension of the domain and the geometry of T such that m(sigma)d_sigma leq D_7 m(T_K,sigma) for all K in T , all sigma in E_ext,K and then using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the L^2(0,T;H^1) estimate (), we obtain left|B_21(delta)-B_210(delta)right| leq delta D_6 sup_s in [m,M]r'(s)sqrtD_1TD_7m(Omega) longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. Estimate of B_22(delta). Since x mapsto xcoth(x) is a 1-Lipschitz continuous function and is equal to 1 in 0, we have left|B_22(delta)right| &leq & sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int fracm(sigma)2left| q_K,sigmaright| left| U_L^n+1-U_K^n+1right| left| psi_L^n-psi_K^nright|\\ & leq & 2delta Vert q Vert_inftysum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int tau_sigmaleft| U_L^n+1-U_K^n+1right| left| psi_L^n-psi_K^nright|, since d_sigma leq 2 delta. Then using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the regularity of psi and the L^2(0,T;H^1) estimate (), there exists D_8>0 only depending on T and Omega such that: left| B_22(delta)right| leq delta Vert qVert_infty D_8 Vert psi Vert_C^1 sqrtD_1 longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. Estimate of B_23(delta). Using Lemma and hypothesis (H4), we have left| dr^n_K,sigma-r'(U^n_K)right| leq sup_s in [m,M]|r''(s)| left|U_L^n-U^n_Kright|, \,\ forall sigma in E_int, \,\ sigma=K|L. Using the regularity of psi and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we obtain left| B_23(delta) right| leq delta sup_s in [m,M]|r''(s)| Vert psi Vert_C^1 sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int tau_sigma left|U_L^n-U^n_Kright| left|U_L^n+1-U^n+1_Kright|, and then using the L^2(0,T;H^1) estimate (), we get left| B_23(delta) right| leq delta sup_s in [m,M]|r''(s)| Vert psi Vert_C^1 D_1 longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. Estimate of B_220(delta). We obtain the same type of estimate as for B_23(delta): left| B_220(delta) right| leq 2delta sup_s in [m,M]|r''(s)| Vert psi Vert_C^1 D_1 longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. Estimate of B_3(delta)-B_30(delta). Using a discrete integration by parts, we obtain B_3(delta) = -sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int m(sigma)q_K,sigmafracU_K^n+1+U_L^n+12left(psi_L^n-psi_K^nright), and then we rewrite B_3(delta) as B_31(delta)+B_32(delta), with B_31(delta)&=&-sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int m(sigma)q_K,sigmafracU_L^n+1-U_K^n+12left(psi_L^n-psi_K^nright),\\ B_32(delta)&=& -sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_int m(sigma)q_K,sigmaU^n+1_Kleft(psi_L^n-psi_K^nright). Using the definition of nabla^deltapsi, we get B_30(delta)=-sum_n=0^N_Tsum_substacksigma in E_intint_t^n^t^n+1int_T_K,sigmau_delta(x,t)fracm(sigma)m(T_K,sigma)left(psi_L^n-psi_K^nright)q(x)cdot n_K,sigma\, dx \, dt, which gives, using the definition of u_delta, B_30(delta)=B_310(delta)+B_320(delta), where B_310(delta) &=& -sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_intm(sigma)left(U^n+1_L-U^n+1_Kright)left(psi_L^n-psi^n_Kright)frac1m(T_K,sigma)int_T_K,sigmacap Lq(x)cdot n_K,sigma\, dx,\\ B_320(delta) &= & -sum_n=0^N_Tsum_substacksigma in E_intm(sigma)U_K^n+1left(psi_L^n-psi^n_Kright)frac1m(T_K,sigma)int_T_K,sigmaq(x)cdot n_K,sigma\, dx. Now we prove that B_32(delta)-B_320(delta) rightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0 and B_31(delta), \, B_310(delta)rightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0.\\ Using the regularity of q, there exists D_9>0 which does not depend on delta such that left| frac1m(sigma)int_sigmaq(x)cdot n_K,sigma \, ds(x)-frac1m(T_K,sigma)int_T_K,sigmaq(x)cdot n_K,sigma \, dxright| leq D_9 delta. Then we can estimate B_32(delta)-B_320(delta): left| B_32(delta)-B_320(delta)right| &leq & delta D_9 M sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_intm(sigma) left|psi_L^n-psi_K^nright|\\ & leq & delta D_8 D_9 M Vert psi Vert_C^1sqrtD_7m(Omega) longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. Moreover, we have left|B_31(delta)right| & leq & delta Vert q Vert_infty sum_n=0^N_TDelta tsum_substacksigma in E_inttau_sigmaleft|U_L^n+1-U_K^n+1right| left|psi_L^n-psi_K^nright|\\ & leq & delta Vert q Vert_infty Vert psi Vert_C^1D_8sqrtD_1 longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0. We obtain in the same way that B_310(delta) longrightarrow 0 as delta rightarrow 0.\\ Hence u satisfies & & int_0^Tint_Omegaleft(u(x,t)\, pa_tpsi(x,t)+r'(u(x,t))\, nabla u(x,t)cdot nablapsi(x,t)+u(x,t)\, q(x)cdot nablapsi(x,t)right)\, dx \, dt\\ & &+int_Omegau(x,0)\, psi(x,0)\, dx=0, and then & & int_0^Tint_Omegaleft(u(x,t)\, pa_tpsi(x,t)+nabla(r(u(x,t)))cdot nablapsi(x,t)+u(x,t)\, q(x)cdot nablapsi(x,t)right)\, dx \, dt\\ & &+int_Omegau(x,0)\, psi(x,0)\, dx=0. nodes.statement: In this article, our aim is to elaborate a finite volume scheme for convection-diffusion equations with nonlinear diffusion. The main objective of building such a scheme is to preserve steady-states in order to be able to apply it to physical models in which it has been proved that the solution converges to equilibrium in long time. In particular, this convergence can be observed in the drift-diffusion system for semiconductors as well as in the porous media equation. \\ In this context, we will first present these two physical models – drift-diffusion system for semiconductors and porous media equation. Then, we will precise the general framework of our study in this article.

To this end, we have to adapt the Scharfetter-Gummel scheme, in such way that ensures that a particular type of steady-state is preserved. Moreover, this new scheme is easier to implement than existing schemes preserving steady-state.\\ In addition, we have shown that there is convergence of our scheme in the nondegenerate case. The proof of this convergence is essentially based on a discrete L^2left(0,T;H^1right) estimate (). A first step to then prove the convergence in the degenerate case would be to show this estimate without using the uniform lower bound of u_delta.\\ Finally, we have observed that this scheme appears to be more accurate than the upwind one, even in the degenerate case. In these two specific cases, we clearly underlined the efficiency of our scheme in order to preserve long-time behavior of the solutions.
